verses.zh: 扫罗登基年四十岁；作以色列王二年的时候，
verses.en: Saul was [thirty][NOTE:1] years old when he began to reign; he ruled over Israel for [forty][NOTE:2] years.
notes: The MT does not have “thirty.” A number appears to have dropped out of the Hebrew text here, since as it stands the MT (literally, “a son of a year”) must mean that Saul was only one year old when he began to reign! The KJV, attempting to resolve this, reads “Saul reigned one year,” but that is not the normal meaning of the Hebrew text represented by the MT. Although most LXX mss lack the entire verse, some Greek mss have “thirty years” here (while others have “one year” like the MT). The Syriac Peshitta has Saul’s age as twenty-one. But this seems impossible to harmonize with the implied age of Saul’s son Jonathan in the following verse. Taking into account the fact that in v. 2 Jonathan was old enough to be a military leader, some scholars prefer to supply in v. 1 the number forty (cf. ASV, NASB). The present translation (“thirty”) is a possible but admittedly uncertain proposal based on a few Greek mss and followed by a number of English versions (e.g., NIV, NCV, NLT). Other English versions simply supply ellipsis marks for the missing number (e.g., NAB, NRSV).

The MT has “two years” here. If this number is to be accepted as correct, the meaning apparently would be that after a lapse of two years at the beginning of Saul’s reign, he then went about the task of consolidating an army as described in what follows (cf. KJV, ASV, CEV). But if the statement in v. 1 is intended to be a comprehensive report on the length of Saul’s reign, the number is too small. According to Acts 13:21 Saul reigned for forty years. Some English versions (e.g., NIV, NCV, NLT), taking this forty to be a round number, add it to the “two years” of the MT and translate the number here as “forty-two years.” While this is an acceptable option, the present translation instead replaces the MT’s “two” with the figure “forty.” Admittedly the textual evidence for this decision is weak, but the same can be said of any attempt to restore sense to this difficult text (note the ellipsis marks at this point in NAB, NRSV). The Syriac Peshitta lacks this part of v. 1.
verses.commentary:
13:1 The MT has "Saul (was). . .years old when he became king and he was king over Israel two years."
The UBS Text Project, p. 171, gives this an "A" rating but obviously a defective text.

Other translations add different numbers.

NASB
"40. . .32"

NKJV
"1. . .2"

REB
"30. . .22"

NET
"30. . .40"

Peshitta
"1 or 2"

This verse is missing in the LXX. JPSOA assumes that the MT has lost two numbers.

- Saul's age at coronation

- how long he reigned; it was some number plus "2," as NASB's "32" or REB's "22"

Paul (quoting Jewish tradition, i.e., Josephus) gives the length of Saul's reign as "40 years" (cf. Acts 13:21).

verses.zh: 就从以色列中拣选了三千人：二千跟随扫罗在密抹和伯特利山，一千跟随约拿单在便雅悯的基比亚；其余的人扫罗都打发各回各家去了。
verses.en: Saul selected for himself 3,000 men from Israel. Of these 2,000 were with Saul at Micmash and in the hill country of Bethel; the remaining 1,000 were with Jonathan at Gibeah in the territory of Benjamin.[NOTE:1] He sent all the rest of the people back home.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “at Gibeah of Benjamin.” The words “in the territory” are supplied in the translation for clarity.
Heb “each one to his tents.”
verses.commentary:
13:2 These were to be Israel's standing army, the rest were volunteers when needed.

▣ "to his tent" This was an idiom for "return home." It went back to the Exodus and Conquest
period, or even before, in the Patriarchal Period.

verses.zh: 约拿单攻击在迦巴的非利士人的防营，非利士人听见了。扫罗就在遍地吹角，意思说，要使希伯来人听见。
verses.en: Jonathan attacked the Philistine outpost[NOTE:1] that was at Geba and the Philistines heard about it. Then Saul alerted[NOTE:2] all the land saying, “Let the Hebrews pay attention!”
notes: Or perhaps “struck down the Philistine official.” See the note at 1 Sam 10:5. Cf. TEV “killed the Philistine commander.”
Heb “blew the ram’s horn in.”
verses.commentary:
13:3 Saul starts a war with the Philistines. He signals all Israel to muster to him for battle.

SPECIAL TOPIC: HORNS USED BY ISRAEL

verses.zh: 以色列众人听见扫罗攻击非利士人的防营，又听见以色列人为非利士人所憎恶，就跟随扫罗聚集在吉甲。
verses.en: All Israel heard this message,[NOTE:1] “Saul has attacked the Philistine outpost, and now Israel is repulsive[NOTE:2] to the Philistines!” So the people were summoned to join[NOTE:3] Saul at Gilgal.
notes: The words “this message” are supplied in the translation for stylistic reasons.
Heb “stinks.” The figurative language indicates that Israel had become repulsive to the Philistines.
Heb “were summoned after.”

The MT has the VERB (BDB 92, KB 107, Niphal PERFECT,
NIDOTTE, vol. 1, pp. 580-581), which means "to smell bad" or "stink" (cf. 2 Sam. 10:6; 16:21).

The Peshitta translates it as parallel to the earlier VERB "had smitten" (BDB 645,
KB 697, Hiphil PERFECT) but no ancient text supports this. Remember, the MT is not the

verses.zh: 非利士人聚集，要与以色列人争战，有车三万辆，马兵六千，步兵像海边的沙那样多，就上来在伯・亚文东边的密抹安营。
verses.en: Meanwhile the Philistines gathered to battle with Israel. Then they went up against Israel[NOTE:1] with 3,000 chariots,[NOTE:2] 6,000 horsemen, and an army as numerous as the sand on the seashore. They went up and camped at Micmash, east of Beth Aven.
notes: The MT omits “they went up against Israel” in a case of homoioteleuton, but these words are preserved in LXX.

The translation follows the Lucianic Greek rescension and the Syriac. Many English versions follow the MT (e.g., KJV, NASB, NRSV, TEV) reading “30,000” here. One expects there to be more horsemen than chariots, cf. 2 Kgs 13:7; 2 Chr 12:3.
verses.commentary:
13:5 Notice how the Philistine army is contrasted to Saul's army (v. 2).

- 30,000 chariots (LXX and NJB, 3,000; some scholars suggest 300)

- 6,000 calvary

- foot soldiers like the sand on the seashore (cf. Josh. 11:4; Jdgs. 7:12; 2 Sam. 17:11)

▣ "chariot" See
SPECIAL TOPIC: CHARIOTS.

verses.zh: 以色列百姓见自己危急窘迫，就藏在山洞、丛林、石穴、隐密处，和坑中。
verses.en: The men of Israel realized they had a problem because their army was hard pressed. So the army hid in caves, thickets, cliffs, strongholds,[NOTE:1] and cisterns.
notes: Or perhaps “vaults.” This rare term also occurs in Judg 9:46, 49. Cf. KJV “high places”; ASV “coverts”; NAB “caverns”; NASB “cellars”; NIV, NCV, TEV “pits”; NRSV, NLT “tombs.”
verses.commentary:
13:6-7 Israel reacted by

- hiding in caves

- hiding in thickets

- hiding in cliffs

- hiding in cellars

- hiding in pits

- running away to Gad

- running away to Gilead

Josephus (Antiq. 6.6.1) says most of the Israelites fled across the Jordan to the tribal lands
of Gad and Reuben.

verses.zh: 有些希伯来人过了约旦河，逃到迦得和基列地。扫罗还是在吉甲，百姓都战战兢兢地跟随他。
verses.en: Some of the Hebrews crossed over the Jordan River[NOTE:1] to the land of Gad and Gilead. But Saul stayed at Gilgal; the entire army that was with him was terrified.
notes: The word “River” is not in the Hebrew text, but has been supplied in the translation for clarity.

verses.zh: 扫罗照着撒母耳所定的日期等了七日。撒母耳还没有来到吉甲，百姓也离开扫罗散去了。
verses.en: He waited for seven days, the time period indicated by Samuel.[NOTE:1] But Samuel did not come to Gilgal, and the army began to abandon Saul.[NOTE:2]
notes: This apparently refers to the instructions given by Samuel in 1 Sam 10:8. If so, several years had passed. On the relationship between chs. 10 and 13, see V. P. Long, The Art of Biblical History (FCI), 201-23.
Heb “dispersed from upon him”; NAB, NRSV “began to slip away.”
verses.commentary: 13:8 Saul was to wait for Samuel seven days (cf. 1 Sam. 10:8).

verses.zh: 扫罗说：「把燔祭和平安祭带到我这里来。」扫罗就献上燔祭。
verses.en: So Saul said, “Bring me the burnt offering and the peace offerings.” Then he offered a burnt offering.

verses.zh: 刚献完燔祭，撒母耳就到了。扫罗出去迎接他，要问他好。
verses.en: Just when he had finished offering the burnt offering, Samuel appeared on the scene. Saul went out to meet him and to greet him.[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “to bless him.”

verses.zh: 撒母耳说：「你做的是甚么事呢？」扫罗说：「因为我见百姓离开我散去，你也不照所定的日期来到，而且非利士人聚集在密抹。
verses.en: But Samuel said, “What have you done?” Saul replied, “When I saw that the army had started to abandon me,[NOTE:1] and that you didn’t come at the appointed time, and that the Philistines had assembled at Micmash,
notes: Heb “dispersed from upon me.”
verses.commentary:
13:11 "What have you done?" The problem was twofold.

- did not obey Samuel's (i.e., YHWH's) word (v. 13)

- offered a sacrifice when he was not authorized (cf. 2 Chr. 26:18)

He surely had good reason based on the situation but it showed a lack of faith in YHWH.

verses.zh: 所以我心里说：恐怕我没有祷告耶和华。非利士人下到吉甲攻击我，我就勉强献上燔祭。」
verses.en: I thought,[NOTE:1] ‘Now the Philistines will come down on me at Gilgal and I have not sought the Lord’s favor.’ So I felt obligated[NOTE:2] to offer the burnt offering.”
notes: Heb “said.”
Or “I forced myself” (so KJV, NASB, NRSV, CEV); NAB “So in my anxiety I offered”; NIV “I felt compelled.”
verses.commentary:
13:12

NASB, NRSV, JPSOA
"So I forced myself"

NKJV, TEV, REB
"I felt compelled"

NJB
"I felt obligated"

Peshitta
"I ventured"

The MT has the VERB (BDB 67, KB 80 II, Hiphil IMPERFECT
with waw) which denotes someone who

- restrains oneself

- feels compelled

This is Saul's first of many excuses why he disobeyed YHWH's expressed will.

verses.zh: 撒母耳对扫罗说：「你做了糊涂事了，没有遵守耶和华―你　神所吩咐你的命令。若遵守，耶和华必在以色列中坚立你的王位，直到永远。
verses.en: Then Samuel said to Saul, “You have made a foolish choice! You have not obeyed[NOTE:1] the commandment that the Lord your God gave[NOTE:2] you. Had you done that, the Lord would have established your kingdom over Israel forever.
notes: Or “kept.”
Heb “commanded.”
verses.commentary:
13:13 "You have acted foolishly" This VERB (BDB 698, KB 754, Niphal
PERFECT) in the Niphal stem is also used in 2 Chr. 16:9).

SPECIAL TOPIC: FOOLISH PEOPLE (terms)

verses.zh: 现在你的王位必不长久。耶和华已经寻着一个合他心意的人，立他作百姓的君，因为你没有遵守耶和华所吩咐你的。」
verses.en: But now your kingdom will not continue. The Lord has sought out[NOTE:1] for himself a man who is loyal to him,[NOTE:2] and the Lord has appointed[NOTE:3] him to be leader over his people, for you have not obeyed what the Lord commanded you.”
notes: This verb form, as well as the one that follows (“appointed”), indicates completed action from the standpoint of the speaker. This does not necessarily mean that the Lord had already conducted his search and made his choice, however. The forms may be used for rhetorical effect to emphasize the certainty of the action. The divine search for a new king is as good as done, emphasizing that the days of Saul’s dynasty are numbered.
Heb “according to his heart.” The idiomatic expression means to be like-minded with another, as its use in 1 Sam 14:7 indicates.
Heb “commanded.”
verses.commentary:
13:14 This is the first of several reasons why Saul is rejected as king.

- disobedient to YHWH's word through Samuel

- disobedient to YHWH by offering a sacrifice

- disobedient by not killing all of the Amalekites and their flocks (1 Samuel 15)

- slaughter of the priests at Nob (1 Samuel 22)

- seeking direction from the witch of Endor (1 Samuel 28)

▣ YHWH was seeking a king who was obedient to His commands. A man with a "whole heart"
(cf. Acts 13:22). When one reads the life of David, this surely does not mean "sinless" or "without faithless acts"!

verses.zh: 撒母耳就起来，从吉甲上到便雅悯的基比亚。扫罗数点跟随他的，约有六百人。
verses.en: Then Samuel set out and went up from Gilgal[NOTE:1] to Gibeah in the territory of Benjamin.[NOTE:2] Saul mustered the army that remained with him; there were about 600 men.
notes: The LXX and two Old Latin mss include the following words here: “on his way. And the rest of the people went up after Saul to meet the warring army. When they arrived from Gilgal….”
Heb “at Gibeah of Benjamin.” The words “in the territory” are supplied in the translation for clarity (likewise in the following verse).

verses.zh: 扫罗和他儿子约拿单，并跟随他们的人，都住在便雅悯的迦巴；但非利士人安营在密抹。
verses.en: Saul, his son Jonathan, and the army that remained with them stayed in Gibeah in the territory of Benjamin, while the Philistines camped in Micmash.[NOTE:1]
notes: The juxtaposition of disjunctive clauses in v. 16 indicates synchronic action.

verses.zh: 有掠兵从非利士营中出来，分为三队：一队往俄弗拉向书亚地去，
verses.en: Raiding bands went out from the camp of the Philistines in three groups. One band turned toward the road leading to Ophrah by the land of Shual;

verses.zh: 一队往伯・和仑去，一队往洗波音谷对面的地境向旷野去。
verses.en: another band turned toward the road leading to Beth Horon; and yet another band turned toward the road leading to the border that overlooks the valley of Zeboyim in the direction of the desert.

verses.zh: 那时，以色列全地没有一个铁匠；因为非利士人说，恐怕希伯来人制造刀枪。
verses.en: A blacksmith could not be found in all the land of Israel, for the Philistines had said, “This will prevent the Hebrews from making swords and spears.”
verses.commentary:
13:19-22 This clearly shows the superior metallurgical knowledge of the Philistines. They had "blacksmiths"
(BDB 360) but Israel had none (1 Sam. 13:22); only Saul and Jonathan had an iron weapon.

verses.zh: 以色列人要磨锄、犁、斧、铲，就下到非利士人那里去磨。
verses.en: So all Israel had to go down to the Philistines in order to get their plowshares, cutting instruments, axes, and sickles[NOTE:1] sharpened.
notes: The translation follows the LXX (“their sickle”) here, rather than the MT “plowshares,” which is due to dittography from the word earlier in the verse.
verses.commentary:
13:20 All of Israel's agricultural implements had to be sharpened by Philistines.

- plowshares (BDB 361)

- mattock (BDB 88 III)

- axe (BDB 899)

- goad (BDB 201)

- forks (BDB 887, v. 21)

verses.zh: 但有锉可以锉铲、犁、三齿叉、斧子，并赶牛锥。
verses.en: They charged[NOTE:1] two-thirds of a shekel[NOTE:2] to sharpen plowshares and cutting instruments, and one-third of a shekel[NOTE:3] to sharpen picks and axes, and to set ox goads.
notes: Heb “the price was.” The meaning of the Hebrew word פְּצִירָה (petsirah) is uncertain. This is the only place it occurs in the OT. Some propose the meaning “sharpening,” but “price” is a more likely meaning if the following term refers to a weight (see the following note on the word “shekel”). See P. K. McCarter, I Samuel (AB), 238.

This word, which appears only here in the OT, probably refers to a stone weight. Stones marked פִּים (pim) have been found in excavations of Palestinian sites. The average weight of such stones is 0.268 ounces, which is equivalent to about two-thirds of a shekel. This probably refers to the price charged by the Philistines for the services listed. See P. K. McCarter, I Samuel (AB), 238; DNWSI 2:910; and G. I. Davies, Ancient Hebrew Inscriptions, 259.
Heb “and for a third, a pick.” The Hebrew text suffers from haplography at this point. The translation follows the textual reconstruction offered by P. K. McCarter, I Samuel (AB), 235.

NKJV, JPSOA, RSV
"pim"

"two-thirds of a shekel"

"one small coin"

The word in the MT (BDB 804, KB 921) is found only here. The root appears on some stones used for
commerce scales in Canaan. The weight of these stones equals about "two-thirds" of a shekel.

The KB calls the root letters (KB 922 II) "thin plate of metal" (cf. Exod. 39:3; Num. 17:3).

Here, it seems to refer to the price the Philistine smiths charged to sharpen the Israeli agricultural
implements. The NET footnote suggests the root may mean "price" and not the specific weight or cost of the service.
Apparently the Philistine smiths charged a large sum!

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this section of
the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

- Why such discrepancy associated with the years of 1 Sam. 13:1?

- Why the unusual name "Hebrews" in 1 Sam. 13:3?

- Why do modern historians think the number "30,000" is too large?

- Why did the men of Israel run from the Philistine army?

- What was Saul's great sin?

- Explain the implication of 1 Sam. 13:19-22.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

NASB (UPDATED) TEXT: 13:1

1Saul was thirty years old when he began to reign, and he reigned thirty-two years over Israel.
